title: Chapter 14 — Some Reflections On American Manners
paragraphs: At first sight nothing seems less important than the outward form of human actions, yet nothing matters more to men: they get used to everything except living in a society whose manners are not their own. The influence of a country’s social and political state on its manners therefore deserves serious examination. Manners are in general the product of the very basis of a people’s character, but they are also sometimes the result of an arbitrary convention among certain men; so they are at once natural and acquired. When certain men see that they are the foremost persons in society, without contest and without effort; when they are constantly occupied with large objects and leave the smaller details to others; and when they live in the enjoyment of wealth they did not amass and do not fear to lose; one may suppose that they feel a kind of haughty disdain for the petty interests and practical cares of life, and that their thoughts take on a natural greatness, which their language and manners show. In democratic countries manners generally lack dignity, because private life there is extremely petty in character; and they are often low, because the mind has few opportunities to rise above the absorbing cares of domestic interests. True dignity in manners consists in always taking one’s proper place, neither too high nor too low; and this is as much within the reach of a peasant as of a prince. In democracies every station appears uncertain. So the manners of democracies, though often full of arrogance, usually lack dignity, and moreover they are never either well disciplined or accomplished.

The men who live in democracies are too unsettled for any number of them ever to succeed in laying down a code of good breeding and forcing people to follow it. Every man therefore behaves in his own way, and there is always a certain incoherence in the manners of such times, because they are shaped by the feelings and ideas of each individual rather than by an ideal model offered for general imitation. This is much more noticeable, however, just after an aristocracy has been overthrown than long after it has been destroyed. New political institutions and new social elements then bring together in the same gathering places, and often force to live in common, men whose education and habits are still amazingly different, and this makes the motley composition of society especially visible. People still remember that a strict code of good breeding once existed, but what it contained or where to find it has already been forgotten. Men have lost the common law of manners, and they have not yet made up their minds to do without it; but everyone tries to build for himself some arbitrary and changeable rule from the remnants of former usages. So manners have neither the regularity and dignity they often show among aristocratic nations, nor the simplicity and freedom they sometimes take on in democracies: they are at once constrained and unconstrained.

This, however, is not the normal state of things. When equality of conditions is long established and complete, all men hold nearly the same ideas and do nearly the same things, so they need not agree or copy one another in order to speak or act in the same way. Their manners are constantly marked by a number of lesser diversities, but not by any great differences. They are never perfectly alike, because they do not copy the same pattern; they are never very unlike, because their social condition is the same. At first sight a traveler would observe that the manners of all Americans are exactly alike; only on close examination can one detect the peculiarities in which they differ.

The English poke fun at the manners of the Americans. It is odd, though, that most of the writers who sketched these ludicrous portraits belonged themselves to the middle classes in England, and the portraits fit those classes perfectly well. These merciless critics thus mostly illustrate the very thing they condemn in the United States. They do not see that they are ridiculing themselves, to the great amusement of the aristocracy of their own country.

Nothing is more harmful to democracy than its outward forms of behavior: many men would willingly put up with its vices who cannot bear its manners. Yet I cannot admit that there is nothing commendable in the manners of a democratic people. Among aristocratic nations, everyone who lives within reach of the first class in society commonly strains to be like it, which gives rise to ridiculous and insipid imitations. A democratic people has no models of high breeding, so at least it is spared the daily sight of wretched copies of them. In democracies manners are never as refined as among aristocratic nations, but on the other hand they are never as coarse. There one hears neither the coarse oaths of the populace nor the elegant and choice expressions of the nobility: the manners of such a people are often vulgar, but they are neither brutal nor mean. I have already observed that in democracies no regular code of good breeding can be laid down; this has some drawbacks and some advantages. In aristocracies the rules of propriety impose the same demeanor on everyone; they make all members of the same class look alike, whatever their private inclinations; they adorn the natural man and they conceal him. Among a democratic people manners are neither so schooled nor so uniform, but they are often more sincere. They form, as it were, a light and loosely woven veil through which the real feelings and private opinions of each individual are easily seen. The form and the substance of human actions therefore often stand in closer relation; and if the great picture of human life is less embellished, it is truer. So it may be said, in one sense, that the effect of democracy is not exactly to give men any particular manners, but to keep them from having manners at all.

The feelings, passions, virtues, and vices of an aristocracy may sometimes reappear in a democracy, but its manners cannot; they are lost, and vanish forever, as soon as the democratic revolution is complete. Nothing seems more lasting than the manners of an aristocratic class, for that class preserves them for some time after it has lost its wealth and power; and nothing seems more fleeting, for no sooner have they disappeared than not a trace of them can be found, and it is scarcely possible to say what they were once they have ceased to be. A change in the state of society works this miracle, and a few generations are enough to complete it. History hands down the principal characteristics of an aristocracy after its destruction, but the light and exquisite touches of its manners are wiped from men’s memories almost as soon as it falls. When men have ceased to see these manners, they can no longer conceive what they were; they are gone, and their departure was unseen and unfelt. For to feel the refined enjoyment that comes from choice and distinguished manners, habit and education must have prepared the heart, and the taste for them is lost almost as easily as the practice of them. Thus a democratic people not only cannot have aristocratic manners, but neither understands nor desires them; and since they have never thought of them, to their minds it is as if such things had never been. Too much importance should not be attached to this loss, but it may well be regretted.

I know that the same men have often joined very refined manners to very base feelings; a look inside the courts shows well enough how imposing an exterior can hide the meanest hearts. Yet even if aristocratic manners were not virtue, they sometimes adorned virtue itself. It was a remarkable sight: a large and powerful class of men whose every outward act seemed guided by a natural loftiness of thought and feeling, by delicate and orderly taste, and by courtesy. Those manners spread a pleasing, illusory charm over human nature. The picture was often false, but no one could look at it without a noble satisfaction.
